This paragraph:

Unlike most street drugs, all samples of SCP-484 are nearly chemically identical. Most illegal drugs vary by manufacturer and contain impurities and additives, but other than cosmetic appearance, SCP-484 samples are identical. The only explanation for this is that all samples come from the same source. Why there is such cosmetic variation is unknown, though researchers believe it is to disguise SCP-484 as a simple street drug. This also explains how a pharmaceutical with the level of sophistication demonstrated

Should be revised for tone. As is, it's quite clumsy.

item.title: Pretty good
item.content:encoded:
I really enjoyed this article, however I can agree with some other commenters about calling him "Crimson Andrew" in the interview. I think a D-class designation would work with a note at the beginning about his "profession" and nickname.

However I don't mind the tone of the interview as other's have remarked. It makes sense to me for a street dealer to attempt to seem tough and gritty, as a persona to play. I imagine that would be how he wants to be seen, and eventually it would likely simply be part of his personality, if it wasn't already.

And while the Doctors normally do have very clinical styles of interviewing, it makes sense to alter the style for the interview. In the end he got the information desired out of Andrew, and that is the important part. If the doctor had give Andrew a bit of slack on his leash to get there, what of it?

item.content:encoded:
I thought it was interesting enough as a concept, but then I got to the interview log at the end. That's a +1 right there. I didn't really see the draw that would make people want to use Vic, but the interview led me to realize that the recreational potential is… different. Literally, "recreation" is an apt description, but I don't think the usual definition applies here.

I have a couple minor gripes. It seems odd that the Foundation would use the guy's nickname throughout the transcript instead of simply mentioning it in the preceding description. Also, the escalation midway through doesn't sit right with me; you'd think the researcher would just answer Andrew's question since it's obvious he has a point to make about it, rather than withholding answers until enough expletives thrown at him. Anyway, this is a Series 1 so I'm assuming that's all staying in, and the core of it is just too good to not upvote.

I see that the redacted section in the containment procedures has been fixed, but otherwise I agree with previous assertions regarding "Crimson Andrew". Either "the subject" or an impromptu D-class designation would be more appropriate.
Also:

Crimson Andrew: You remember your fifth birthday?
Dr. ██████: I don't see how that's relevant.
Crimson Andrew: Just, fuck, do you remember or not?
Dr. ██████: Yes, I do.
Crimson Andrew: How was it?
Dr. ██████: I really don't…
Crimson Andrew: (shouting) How the fuck was it?
Dr. ██████: It was very nice.

It may just be me, but it seems odd that any Foundation interrogation would allow a drug dealer to turn the tables and start barking questions back. It lends itself well to the log as a whole, 'telling the story' and being a well written portion that adds to the page as a whole (bollocks to the guidelines, is what that means), I just thought I'd point that out. Definitely upvoted.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: The purpose of describing its chemical purity and its manufacture were to point out in an indirect way it was produced by a central source toward some to-date unknown purpose. No megacorp or shady cabal produces something like this and sells it as a street drug just for kicks. Wondering WHY there is cosmetic variation is meant to make the reader wonder what else they don't know about its purpose. As for the slang descriptions, that was more to emphasize how many people in the world not only are aware of this SCP, but of its actual effects. Imagine an SCP well known enough to have its own slang, albeit within the more limited confines of drug culture. That was meant to suggest the difficulty of achieving the Contain in SCP, since it's reached a (comparatively) high level of exposure, presumably by design. Of course, if it is too wordy to convey that, it may well do with some condensing.
